entities.name: Classic of Changes (Yijing / I Ching)
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The oldest of the Five Confucian Classics (Wujing) and one of the oldest Chinese texts in continuous use, dating in its earliest layers to the Western Zhou period (c. 1000–750 BCE) with later philosophical commentary (the "Ten Wings") added through the Warring States and Han periods. The Yijing is organized around 64 hexagrams — six-line figures composed of broken (yin) and unbroken (yang) lines — each with associated judgments, line texts, and commentaries.

Originally a divination manual (consulting the hexagrams through yarrow stalks or coins), it evolved into a comprehensive cosmological and philosophical system describing the dynamic interplay of complementary forces (yin-yang), the processes of change, and the patterns underlying all phenomena. Leibniz saw in the hexagram system a prefiguration of his binary arithmetic (0 and 1).

The Yijing influenced Chinese philosophy, science, medicine, military strategy, and art for three millennia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Classic of Changes has shaped Chinese philosophy and cosmology for millennia, influencing Confucianism, Taoism, and Buddhism. Its concepts of yin-yang and the cyclical nature of change have had a lasting impact on East Asian thought.
